title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
hints: Use a hash map to store values you have seen.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string of brackets, determine whether it is valid.
hints: A stack matches the most recent opening bracket.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
hints: Track the last index of each character with two pointers.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
hints: A min-heap keeps the smallest head available.

title: Print Hello World
statement: Given a string name, return the greeting Hello, <name>! built from it: the word Hello, a comma, a space, the name, and an exclamation mark. For example the name World gives Hello, World! (capital H, no extra spaces). Printing Hello World is recast as returning this string.
hints: Return the string instead of printing it.
Join the pieces with string concatenation or a template literal.

title: Check Even or Odd
statement: Given an integer n, return the string "Even" if n is divisible by 2, otherwise return the string "Odd". Zero is even and negative numbers are handled the same way.
hints: Use the remainder operator %.
For negative numbers n % 2 can be -1, so compare against 0 instead of 1.

title: Find the Largest of Two Numbers
statement: Given two integers a and b, return the larger of the two. If they are equal, return that value.
hints: Compare the two numbers with an if statement.
Equal numbers need no special case.

title: Find the Largest of Three Numbers
statement: Given three integers a, b and c, return the largest of the three. If several are equal to the maximum, return that value.
hints: Keep a running maximum and compare it with each number.
Equal values are fine, the maximum is still the same number.

title: Check Positive, Negative or Zero
statement: Given an integer n, return the string "Positive" if n > 0, "Negative" if n < 0, or "Zero" if n == 0.
hints: Use if / else if / else.
Return the strings with the exact capitalization shown.

title: Swap Two Numbers
statement: Given two integers a and b, return an array of two elements with their values swapped, that is [b, a].
hints: You can use a temporary variable, or simply build the array in the new order.
The returned array must have exactly two elements.

title: Find Factorial of a Number
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return n! (n factorial), the product of all integers from 1 to n. By definition 0! = 1.
hints: Start with result = 1 and multiply by every i from 2 to n.
0! and 1! are both 1.

title: Check Prime Number
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return true if n is a prime number and false otherwise. A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. So 0 and 1 are not prime.
hints: Numbers below 2 are not prime.
You only need to test divisors up to the square root of n.

title: Print Fibonacci Series
statement: Given an integer n, return an array containing the first n terms of the Fibonacci series, starting with 0, 1. Each later term is the sum of the previous two. If n is 0 return an empty array.
hints: Keep the last two terms in variables and update them in a loop.
Handle n = 0 and n = 1 separately if needed.

title: Reverse a Number
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return the number formed by reversing its digits. Leading zeros of the result are dropped because the result is a number, for example 1200 becomes 21.
hints: Repeatedly take n % 10 and append it to the result with result = result * 10 + digit.
Divide n by 10 (integer division) each step.

title: Check Palindrome Number
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return true if its decimal digits read the same forwards and backwards, otherwise return false. For example 121 is a palindrome and 120 is not.
hints: Reverse the number and compare it with the original.
Single digit numbers are palindromes.

title: Find Sum of Digits
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return the sum of its decimal digits. For example the digits of 1234 add up to 10.
hints: n % 10 gives the last digit.
Integer-divide n by 10 to drop the last digit.

title: Count Digits in a Number
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return how many digits it has in decimal. The number 0 has exactly 1 digit.
hints: Divide by 10 repeatedly and count the steps.
Treat 0 as a special case.

title: Check Armstrong Number
statement: A number is an Armstrong number if the sum of each of its digits raised to the power of the number of digits equals the number itself. For example 153 = 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3. Given a non-negative integer n, return true if it is an Armstrong number, otherwise false.
hints: First count the digits, then sum digit^count.
Single digit numbers (including 0) are Armstrong numbers.

title: Find GCD and LCM
statement: Given two positive integers a and b, return an array [gcd, lcm] where gcd is their greatest common divisor and lcm is their least common multiple.
hints: Use the Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b).
lcm = a / gcd * b.

title: Find Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given a non-empty array of integers nums, return the largest value in it.
hints: Start with the first element as the current maximum.
Scan the rest and update when you find a bigger one.

title: Find Smallest Element in an Array
statement: Given a non-empty array of integers nums, return the smallest value in it.
hints: Start with the first element as the current minimum.
Scan the rest and update when you find a smaller one.

title: Find Second Largest Element
statement: Given an array of integers nums, return the second largest distinct value, that is the largest value that is strictly smaller than the maximum. If the array has fewer than two distinct values, return -1.
constraints: 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^9 (so -1 can never be a real answer)
hints: Track the largest and second largest in a single pass.
Ignore elements equal to the current largest so duplicates do not count.

title: Reverse an Array
statement: Given an array of integers nums, return a new array containing the same elements in reverse order. An empty array stays empty.
hints: Swap elements from both ends moving inwards.
Or build the result by reading nums from the last index to the first.

title: Calculate Sum of Array Elements
statement: Given an array of integers nums, return the sum of all its elements. The sum of an empty array is 0.
hints: Keep a running total starting at 0.
The empty array needs no special handling with a running total.

title: Find Duplicate Elements
statement: Given an array of integers nums, return a sorted (ascending) array of the distinct values that appear more than once in nums. Each such value appears exactly once in the result. If no value is repeated, return an empty array.
hints: Count occurrences with a hash map.
Collect values whose count is at least 2, then sort them numerically.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement: Given an array of integers nums sorted in non-decreasing order, return a new array containing each distinct value exactly once, keeping the sorted order (the compacted array without duplicates). An empty array returns an empty array.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Use two pointers: one reads, one marks where the next unique value goes.
A value is new when it differs from the previous element.

title: Move All Zeros to End
statement: Given an array of integers nums, return a new array in which all zeros are moved to the end while the relative order of the non-zero elements is kept. The length stays the same.
hints: Write non-zero values forward with a write pointer, then fill the rest with zeros.
Do not sort; order of non-zero elements must be preserved.

title: Rotate Array by K Positions
statement: Given an array of integers nums and a non-negative integer k, return a new array that is nums rotated to the right by k positions. For example [1,2,3,4,5] rotated by 2 is [4,5,1,2,3]. k may be larger than the array length. An empty array stays empty.
hints: Rotating by the length returns the original array, so use k % n.
The last k elements move to the front.

title: Find Missing Number
statement: Given an array nums containing n distinct integers taken from the range 0 to n inclusive (in any order), exactly one number from that range is missing. Return the missing number.
hints: The sum of 0..n is n * (n + 1) / 2; subtract the array sum.
XOR of all indices and values also works.

title: Find Frequency of Each Element
statement: Given an array of integers nums, count how many times each distinct value appears. Return an array of [value, count] pairs, one pair per distinct value, sorted by value in ascending order.
hints: Use a map from value to count.
Sort the distinct values numerically before building the result.

title: Find Pair with Given Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, find indices i and j with i < j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. If several pairs exist, return the lexicographically smallest [i, j] (smallest i first, then smallest j). If no pair exists, return [-1, -1].
hints: A double loop with i < j visits pairs in lexicographic order already.
A hash map can find the complement in O(n) but be careful to keep the smallest i.

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Given two integer arrays a and b, each sorted in non-decreasing order, return a single array containing all elements of both arrays, sorted in non-decreasing order. Duplicates are kept.
hints: Keep one pointer in each array and always take the smaller current element.
Append the leftovers once one array is exhausted.

title: Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm)
statement: Given a non-empty array of integers nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one element) with the largest sum and return that sum.
hints: Track the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index.
At each element, either extend the previous subarray or start fresh.

title: Sort an Array of 0s, 1s and 2s
statement: Given an array nums containing only the values 0, 1 and 2, return the array sorted in ascending order (all 0s, then all 1s, then all 2s). Try to do it in a single pass (Dutch national flag).
hints: Keep three regions using low, mid and high pointers.
Counting each value and rebuilding also works.

title: Reverse a String
statement: Given a string s, return a new string with the characters of s in reverse order. All characters, including spaces, are kept.
hints: Walk from the last index to the first and build the result.
Two pointers swapping from both ends also works.

title: Check Palindrome String
statement: Given a string s, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise false. The comparison is case-sensitive and every character (including spaces and punctuation) counts. An empty string is a palindrome.
hints: Compare s[i] with s[n-1-i] for the first half.
Or compare s with its reverse.

title: Count Vowels and Consonants
statement: Given a string s, return [vowels, consonants] where vowels is the number of letters in s that are a, e, i, o or u (case-insensitive) and consonants is the number of other English letters (a-z, A-Z). Digits, spaces and symbols are ignored.
hints: Lowercase each character first.
Check whether it is a letter before deciding vowel or consonant.

title: Find Duplicate Characters
statement: Given a string s, return an array of the characters that appear more than once in s. Each such character appears once in the result as a 1-character string, and the result is sorted by character code in ascending order. The comparison is case-sensitive and spaces count as characters. If there are none, return an empty array.
hints: Count occurrences of each character.
Keep those with count > 1 and sort them.

title: Find First Non-Repeating Character
statement: Given a string s, return the first character (reading left to right) that appears exactly once in s, as a 1-character string. If no such character exists, return the empty string "". The comparison is case-sensitive.
hints: Count characters in a first pass.
Scan again and return the first one with count 1.

title: Check Anagram Strings
statement: Given two strings a and b, return true if b is an anagram of a, meaning b can be formed by rearranging all the characters of a using each character exactly as many times as it appears. The comparison is case-sensitive and spaces count as characters. Otherwise return false.
hints: If the lengths differ the answer is false.
Compare character counts, or compare the sorted strings.

title: Remove Spaces from String
statement: Given a string s, return a new string with every space character (" ") removed. All other characters keep their original order.
hints: Build the result by skipping characters equal to a space.

title: Find Frequency of Characters
statement: Given a string s, return an array of [char, count] pairs, one pair per distinct character in s, where char is a 1-character string and count is how many times it appears. Sort the pairs by character code in ascending order. The comparison is case-sensitive and spaces count as characters.
hints: Use a map from character to count.
Sort the distinct characters by their character code.

title: Reverse Words in a Sentence
statement: Given a sentence s made of words separated by single spaces (no leading or trailing spaces), return the sentence with the order of the words reversed. The letters inside each word stay as they are, and words in the result are separated by single spaces. An empty sentence returns an empty string.
constraints: Words are separated by exactly one space
s has no leading or trailing spaces
hints: Split the sentence on spaces.
Reverse the list of words and join with a space.

title: Longest Common Prefix
statement: Given an array of strings strs, return the longest string that is a prefix of every string in the array. If there is no common prefix, return the empty string "". If strs is empty, return "".
hints: Start with the first string as the prefix.
Shorten it until every other string starts with it.

title: Linear Search
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, scan the array from left to right and return the index of the first element equal to target. If target is not present, return -1.
hints: Check each element in order and stop at the first match.

title: Binary Search
statement: Given an integer array nums sorted in strictly ascending order (all values distinct) and an integer target, return the index of target in nums using binary search. If target is not present, return -1.
hints: Keep lo and hi bounds and look at the middle element.
Discard the half that cannot contain target.

title: First and Last Position of Element
statement: Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order (duplicates allowed) and an integer target, return [first, last] where first and last are the lowest and highest indices at which target appears. If target is not present, return [-1, -1].
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Run a binary search twice: once for the leftmost and once for the rightmost position.
When you find a match, keep searching on one side.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A strictly ascending array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot, for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] may become [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Given the rotated array nums and an integer target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is not present. Aim for O(log n) time.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
hints: At every step, one half of the current range is sorted.
Check whether target lies inside the sorted half to choose which half to keep.

title: Bubble Sort
statement: Sort the integer array nums in ascending order using bubble sort (repeatedly swap adjacent elements that are out of order) and return the sorted array.
hints: After each pass the largest remaining element reaches its final position.
Stop early if a pass makes no swaps.

title: Selection Sort
statement: Sort the integer array nums in ascending order using selection sort (repeatedly select the minimum of the unsorted part and move it to the front) and return the sorted array.
hints: For each position i, find the index of the smallest element in nums[i..].
Swap it into position i.

title: Insertion Sort
statement: Sort the integer array nums in ascending order using insertion sort (grow a sorted prefix by inserting each next element into its correct place) and return the sorted array.
hints: Take nums[i] as a key and shift larger elements of the sorted prefix one step right.
Drop the key into the gap.

title: Merge Sort
statement: Sort the integer array nums in ascending order using merge sort (split in halves, sort each half recursively, then merge) and return the sorted array.
hints: The base case is an array of length 0 or 1.
Merging two sorted halves takes linear time with two pointers.

title: Quick Sort
statement: Sort the integer array nums in ascending order using quick sort (pick a pivot, partition the elements around it, and sort the two sides recursively) and return the sorted array.
hints: Partition so that smaller elements come before the pivot and larger ones after.
Recurse on the left and right parts.

title: Find Kth Largest Element
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest value in nums, where k = 1 means the largest. Duplicates are counted separately: in [3,3,2], the 1st and 2nd largest are both 3 and the 3rd largest is 2.
hints: Sorting in descending order and taking index k-1 works.
A min-heap of size k or quickselect is faster.

title: Create a Linked List
statement: You start with an empty singly linked list. Given an array values, insert each value one by one at the HEAD of the list, in the given order (first value first). After all insertions, return the list read from head to tail as an array. A linked list is represented as an array of its values, head first.
hints: Each insertion at the head makes the new node the first node.
The last inserted value ends up at the head.

title: Insert Node at Beginning
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Insert a new node holding the value x at the beginning of the list and return the resulting list as an array (head first).
hints: The new node becomes the new head and points to the old head.

title: Insert Node at End
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Insert a new node holding the value x at the end (tail) of the list and return the resulting list as an array (head first).
hints: Walk to the last node and attach the new node.
Handle the empty list: the new node becomes the head.

title: Delete a Node
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Delete the FIRST node whose value equals x and return the resulting list as an array. If no node holds x, return the list unchanged.
hints: Deleting the head is a special case.
Keep a pointer to the previous node so you can relink around the deleted one.

title: Search an Element
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Return the 0-based position of the first node whose value equals x, counting from the head. If no node holds x, return -1.
hints: Traverse from the head while counting the index.
Stop at the first match.

title: Reverse a Linked List
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Reverse the list by reversing the direction of its links and return the reversed list as an array (head first).
hints: Keep prev, curr and next pointers.
Point each node to the previous one while walking forward.

title: Find Middle of Linked List
statement: A non-empty singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Return the value of its middle node. If the list has an even number of nodes there are two middle nodes; return the value of the SECOND one.
hints: Move a slow pointer by one and a fast pointer by two.
When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

title: Detect Cycle in Linked List
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). The integer pos tells where the tail node links to: the tail's next pointer points to the node at 0-based index pos. If pos is -1, the tail points to nothing and there is no cycle. Return true if the list contains a cycle, otherwise false.
constraints: pos is -1 when values is empty
hints: Floyd cycle detection: a slow pointer moves 1 step, a fast pointer 2 steps.
If they ever meet there is a cycle; if fast reaches the end there is none.

title: Remove Nth Node from End
statement: A singly linked list is given as an array values (head first). Remove the n-th node counting from the END of the list (n = 1 is the last node) and return the resulting list as an array (head first).
hints: Advance a fast pointer n steps ahead, then move both pointers together.
Removing the head is a special case; a dummy node helps.

title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
statement: Two singly linked lists a and b are given as arrays (head first), each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge them into one sorted list and return it as an array (head first).
constraints: both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Compare the two current heads and take the smaller one.
When one list runs out, append the rest of the other.

title: Implement Stack Using Array
statement: Implement a stack (last in, first out) backed by an array, then run a sequence of operations on it. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "push" (argument: a value to push; result -1), "pop" (remove and return the top value, or -1 if the stack is empty), "peek" (return the top value without removing it, or -1 if empty), "isEmpty" (return 1 if the stack is empty, else 0), "size" (return the number of elements). Return the array of results, one per operation. Pushed values are non-negative.
hints: Use an array and its end as the top of the stack.
Check for emptiness before pop and peek.

title: Implement Queue Using Array
statement: Implement a queue (first in, first out) backed by an array, then run a sequence of operations on it. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "enqueue" (argument: a value to add at the back; result -1), "dequeue" (remove and return the front value, or -1 if the queue is empty), "front" (return the front value without removing it, or -1 if empty), "isEmpty" (return 1 if empty, else 0), "size" (return the number of elements). Return the array of results, one per operation. Enqueued values are non-negative.
hints: Keep an array plus a front index, or use shift().
Check for emptiness before dequeue and front.

title: Implement Stack Using Linked List
statement: Implement a stack using a singly linked list (the head is the top), then run a sequence of operations. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "push" (argument: a value; inserts a new head node and returns the NEW size of the stack), "pop" (remove the head and return its value, or -1 if empty), "top" (return the head value without removing it, or -1 if empty), "isEmpty" (1 if empty, else 0), "size" (number of nodes). Return the array of results, one per operation. Pushed values are non-negative.
hints: Push: create a node whose next is the old head, then make it the head.
Keep a counter for the size.

title: Implement Queue Using Linked List
statement: Implement a queue using a singly linked list with head and tail pointers, then run a sequence of operations. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "enqueue" (argument: a value; appends a node at the tail and returns the NEW size of the queue), "dequeue" (remove the head and return its value, or -1 if empty), "front" (return the head value without removing it, or -1 if empty), "isEmpty" (1 if empty, else 0), "size" (number of nodes). Return the array of results, one per operation. Enqueued values are non-negative.
hints: Enqueue at the tail, dequeue from the head.
When the last node is dequeued, the tail must also become empty.

title: Next Greater Element
statement: Given an array nums, return an array res of the same length where res[i] is the first element to the right of index i that is strictly greater than nums[i]. If there is no such element, res[i] is -1.
hints: A brute force double loop is O(n^2).
Keep a stack of indices whose answer is not found yet; when a bigger value arrives, pop and resolve them.

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack that supports retrieving its minimum element in constant time, then run a sequence of operations. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "push" (argument: a value; result -1), "pop" (remove the top and return it, or -1 if empty), "top" (return the top without removing it, or -1 if empty), "getMin" (return the minimum value currently in the stack, or -1 if empty). Return the array of results, one per operation. Pushed values are non-negative.
hints: Store, with each element, the minimum of the stack up to that element.
Or keep a second stack of minimums.

title: Implement Queue Using Two Stacks
statement: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks, then run a sequence of operations. ops[i] is the operation name and values[i] is its argument list (empty if none). Operations: "push" (argument: a value added to the back of the queue; result -1), "pop" (remove and return the front element, or -1 if the queue is empty), "peek" (return the front element without removing it, or -1 if empty), "empty" (return 1 if the queue is empty, else 0). Return the array of results, one per operation. Pushed values are non-negative.
hints: Push onto an input stack.
When the output stack is empty, move everything from the input stack onto it; this reverses the order.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Given an integer array nums and a window size k, a window of k consecutive elements slides from the left end to the right end of the array, one position at a time. Return an array containing the maximum of each window, in order. The result has nums.length - k + 1 elements.
hints: Brute force is O(n*k).
Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order; the front is always the window maximum.
Drop the front when it leaves the window.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Given an array heights where heights[i] is the height of the i-th bar of a histogram and every bar has width 1, return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram (the rectangle is made of consecutive bars).
hints: For each bar, find how far left and right it can extend while staying the minimum.
A stack of increasing heights finds those boundaries in one pass; append a 0 bar at the end to flush the stack.

title: Factorial Using Recursion
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return n! (n factorial) computed recursively. n! = n * (n-1)!, and 0! = 1.
hints: Base case: n is 0 or 1 returns 1.
Recursive case: n * factorial(n - 1).

title: Fibonacci Using Recursion
statement: Given a non-negative integer n, return the n-th Fibonacci number computed recursively, where F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2).
hints: Two base cases: F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1.
The plain recursion is exponential; memoization makes it linear.

title: Sum of Array Using Recursion
statement: Given an integer array nums, return the sum of all its elements computed recursively (the sum of an empty array is 0).
hints: Base case: an empty array sums to 0.
sum(nums, i) = nums[i] + sum(nums, i + 1).

title: Reverse String Using Recursion
statement: Given a string s, return the string reversed, computed recursively (for example, "abc" becomes "cba"). The empty string stays empty.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters
hints: Base case: an empty string returns itself.
reverse(s) = reverse(s without its first character) + first character.

title: Generate All Subsets
statement: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set), including the empty subset. Each subset must list its elements in ascending order. Return the list of subsets sorted lexicographically: compare subsets element by element, and a subset that is a prefix of another comes first (so the empty subset is first).
constraints: all elements of nums are distinct
hints: For each element decide: include it or skip it.
Sort nums first; backtracking in index order then produces subsets already in lexicographic order.

title: Generate All Permutations
statement: Given an array nums of distinct non-negative integers, return every possible permutation (ordering) of its elements as an array of arrays. The list of permutations must be sorted lexicographically: compare two permutations element by element as numbers, and the first position where they differ decides which comes first.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
hints: Build a permutation one position at a time, tracking which elements are already used.
Backtrack: choose an unused element, recurse, then undo the choice.
If you sort nums first and try elements in order, results come out already sorted.

title: Combination Sum
statement: Given an array candidates of distinct positive integers and a positive integer target, return all unique combinations of candidates whose sum equals target. Each candidate may be used any number of times. Two combinations are the same if they use each number the same number of times, so order inside a combination does not matter: write every combination in ascending order. Return the list of combinations sorted lexicographically (compare element by element as numbers; a shorter combination that is a prefix of a longer one comes first). If no combination exists, return an empty array.
hints: Sort the candidates, then at each step decide which candidate index to use next.
Recurse with the same index to allow reuse; move to a later index to avoid duplicate combinations.
Stop exploring when the remaining target becomes negative.

title: Rat in a Maze
statement: A rat starts at the top-left cell of a grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. The grid maze is an array of rows where 1 means an open cell and 0 means a blocked cell. The rat may move Down (D), Left (L), Right (R) or Up (U) into an open cell inside the grid, and it must never visit the same cell twice within a single path. Return all possible paths as strings of moves (for example "DDRR"), sorted in lexicographic (alphabetical) order. If the start or end cell is blocked, or no path exists, return an empty array. If the grid is a single open cell, the only path is the empty string, so return [""].
hints: Use DFS with a visited marker for the current path.
Try the moves in the order D, L, R, U; then the collected paths come out sorted.
Unmark a cell when you backtrack out of it.

title: N-Queens Problem
statement: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal). Given the integer n, return the number of distinct ways to place the queens. If no placement exists, return 0.
hints: Place one queen per row and choose its column.
Track used columns and both diagonals (row - col and row + col) in sets or arrays.
Backtrack after exploring each column choice.

title: Sudoku Solver
statement: Given a 9 x 9 Sudoku board as an array of 9 rows of 9 integers, where 0 means an empty cell and 1-9 are given digits, fill the empty cells so that every row, every column and every 3 x 3 box contains each digit 1-9 exactly once. Return the completed board in the same format. Every input puzzle has exactly one solution.
constraints: The puzzle has exactly one valid solution
hints: Find the next empty cell and try digits 1 to 9 that do not conflict with its row, column or box.
Recurse; if a branch fails, reset the cell to 0 and try the next digit.
Return as soon as one branch fills the whole board.

title: Binary Tree Traversals
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Node values are non-negative. For example [1,2,3,-1,4] is a root 1 with left child 2 and right child 3, where 2 has no left child and has right child 4. Return an array of three arrays [inorder, preorder, postorder] holding the node values of the three depth-first traversals. An empty tree [] gives [[],[],[]].
constraints: Node values are non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: First build node objects from the level-order array using a queue.
Inorder: left, node, right. Preorder: node, left, right. Postorder: left, right, node.

title: Find Height of Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Node values are non-negative. Return the height of the tree, defined as the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree [] has height 0.
constraints: Node values are non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: Height of a node = 1 + max(height of left, height of right).
An absent node has height 0.

title: Count Nodes in Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Node values are non-negative. Return the total number of nodes in the tree. An empty tree [] has 0 nodes. Note that -1 entries are placeholders, not nodes.
constraints: Node values are non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: Count = 1 + count(left) + count(right), and 0 for an absent node.
Build the tree with a queue before recursing.

title: Level Order Traversal
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Node values are non-negative. Return the level order traversal as an array of arrays: one inner array per depth, listing that level's node values from left to right. An empty tree [] returns [].
constraints: Node values are non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: Use a queue; process exactly queue.length nodes for each level.
Push the left then right child of every node you process.

title: Check Balanced Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Node values are non-negative. A tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return true if the tree is height-balanced, otherwise false. An empty tree [] is balanced.
constraints: Node values are non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: Compute heights bottom-up and compare at every node.
Return a sentinel such as -1 from the height function as soon as an imbalance is found, to avoid recomputation.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor
statement: A general binary tree (not necessarily a search tree) is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). All node values are distinct non-negative integers, and both p and q are values present in the tree. Return the value of the lowest common ancestor of p and q: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree, where a node counts as a descendant of itself. If p equals q, the answer is p.
constraints: Node values are distinct non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
p and q exist in the tree
hints: Recurse: if the current node is p or q, return it.
If both the left and right recursive calls find something, the current node is the LCA.
Otherwise return whichever side found something.

title: Binary Search Tree Search
statement: A binary search tree (all values in the left subtree are smaller than a node, all values in the right subtree are larger; values are distinct and non-negative) is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). Search for the node whose value equals target. Return the subtree rooted at that node, written in the same level-order format: list nodes level by level, giving each existing node's left and right child (using -1 for an absent child), and remove trailing -1 values at the end. If target is not in the tree, return an empty array [].
constraints: Node values are distinct non-negative integers; -1 marks an absent node
hints: Walk down from the root: go left if target is smaller, right if larger.
Once found, run a level-order walk from that node, writing -1 for each missing child, then trim trailing -1 values.

title: Graph BFS
statement: An undirected graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n-1 and is given as an edge list: each edge [u, v] connects u and v in both directions. Starting from node start, perform a breadth-first search, always visiting the neighbours of a node in ascending order of node number. Return the array of nodes in the order they are first visited. Only nodes reachable from start appear in the answer.
hints: Build an adjacency list and sort each list ascending.
Use a queue and mark a node visited when you enqueue it.

title: Graph DFS
statement: An undirected graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n-1 and is given as an edge list: each edge [u, v] connects u and v in both directions. Starting from node start, perform a depth-first search, always exploring the neighbours of a node in ascending order of node number and going as deep as possible before backtracking. Return the array of nodes in the order they are first visited (preorder). Only nodes reachable from start appear in the answer.
hints: Build an adjacency list and sort each list ascending.
Recurse into each unvisited neighbour; mark a node visited when you first enter it.

title: Detect Cycle in Graph
statement: An undirected graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n-1 and is given as an edge list: each edge [u, v] connects u and v in both directions. The graph may be disconnected. Return true if the graph contains at least one cycle (a path of three or more distinct nodes that returns to its starting node), otherwise return false.
hints: Union-Find: if an edge joins two nodes already in the same set, there is a cycle.
Alternatively run DFS from every unvisited node and remember the parent; meeting a visited non-parent neighbour means a cycle.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each move you may climb either 1 or 2 steps. Given n, return the number of distinct sequences of moves that take you exactly to the top. For n = 0 there is exactly one way (do nothing).
hints: The ways to reach step i come from step i-1 or step i-2.
ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2], like Fibonacci.

title: House Robber
statement: A row of houses holds the amounts of money given in the array nums (nums[i] is the money in house i). You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum total amount you can rob. If there are no houses, return 0.
hints: For each house choose: skip it (keep the best so far) or rob it (best from two houses back plus its money).
Only the previous two values are needed.

title: Coin Change
statement: Given an array coins of positive coin denominations (each can be used any number of times) and a non-negative integer amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make exactly that amount. If it is impossible, return -1. For amount 0 the answer is 0.
hints: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins for amount a; dp[0] = 0.
dp[a] = min over coins c <= a of dp[a - c] + 1.
Greedy does not always work, e.g. coins [1,3,4] and amount 6.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings a and b, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence keeps the relative order of characters but may skip characters (it need not be contiguous). If the strings share no characters, or one is empty, return 0.
hints: dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b.
If a[i-1] == b[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise take the max of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (a sequence of elements in original order, not necessarily contiguous, where each element is strictly greater than the previous). For an empty array return 0.
hints: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i.
dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
A faster O(n log n) approach uses a "tails" array and binary search.

title: 0/1 Knapsack
statement: You have n items; item i has weight weights[i] and value values[i]. A knapsack can carry total weight at most capacity. Each item can be taken at most once (0/1). Return the maximum total value you can carry.
constraints: weights and values have the same length
hints: dp[w] = best value using capacity w.
Process items one by one and iterate w from capacity down to the item weight so each item is used once.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
statement: You are given a chain of matrices to multiply in order. The array dims describes them: matrix i has dims[i] rows and dims[i+1] columns, so there are dims.length - 1 matrices. Multiplying a matrix of size p x q by one of size q x r costs p * q * r scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative, so you may choose any parenthesization. Return the minimum total number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the whole product. With a single matrix the cost is 0.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the min cost to multiply matrices i..j.
Try every split point k: dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + dims[i] * dims[k+1] * dims[j+1].
Fill by increasing chain length.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of single-character operations needed to convert a into b. The allowed operations are: insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character. Either string may be empty.
hints: dp[i][j] = edit distance between the first i characters of a and the first j of b.
Base cases: dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j.
If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).

title: Word Break Problem
statement: Given a string s and an array of words (a dictionary), return true if s can be split into a sequence of one or more dictionary words concatenated together with no leftover characters, otherwise return false. Dictionary words may be reused any number of times. An empty string s can always be formed (return true).
constraints: All strings are lowercase English letters
hints: dp[i] is true if the first i characters can be segmented; dp[0] = true.
dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s.slice(j, i) is in the dictionary.

title: Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array: the first value is the root, and then, going level by level and left to right, each existing node is followed by its left child and right child, where -1 means that child is absent (absent nodes have no children listed). All node values are non-negative. A path is any sequence of connected nodes that follows parent-child edges, visits each node at most once, and may start and end at any node (it does not need to pass through the root). Return the largest possible sum of node values along such a path. An empty tree [] returns 0.
constraints: Node values are integers between 0 and 1000; -1 marks an absent node
hints: For each node compute the best downward path starting at it: value + max(left gain, right gain).
The best path that bends at a node is value + left gain + right gain; track the maximum over all nodes.
